The Tyranny Of Structure
Amir Husain, Forbes, 2021-05-13

Organizational structures are at the heart of human endeavor and reflect deeply in human institutions. There is a particularly pronounced tension today between the two principal styles of organizational structures; centralized and distributed. There is no explanation necessary as to what centralized structures look like. We’ve seen them and interacted with them. The Federal Government, most major financial institutions, including Central Banks, and conventional militaries. These are all examples of centralized organizations. But centralization is not merely a hallmark of institutions. It is also a design feature in large scale systems that are at the core of great volumes of economic activity. For example, take the Google search engine. It is but another example of a centralized system; one that collects information from all over the web and maintains it in a centralized database, run by a single company and governed by a small group of executives, developers, and information technology experts. Most of the cloudbased services in vogue today are all centralized systems. Even though they may have components distributed minimally across geographies for reasons of performance, their information structures, control mechanisms and governance mechanisms all remain central.

And what of distributed organizations and structures? From the financial world we can identify two examples of distributed systems that have occupied headlines recently. The first is a decentralized store of value, the Bitcoin cryptocurrency. This is both a medium of low-frequency exchange and a high-volume store of value that requires no centralized authority to function. It can be “mined” or produced by anyone who is plugged into the peer-to-peer bitcoin network, who follows the rules and performs the computations required to be a bitcoin participant. All are equal in a system of this type and no one entity exercises greater authority than any other participating entity. Another example from the world of finance is the WallStreetBets (WSB) “distributed hedge fund” community on Reddit. This is a gathering of hundreds of thousands of mostly small, retail investors who each form their own opinions, but can be influenced by an open flow of ideas, opinions and information shared with them by other WSB participants. No one can force the WSB community to act a certain way, but a consensus amongst them can indeed emerge. What results from such a consensus can be a powerful economic force, as was demonstrated in the recent GameStop (GME) short squeeze incident.

Distributed systems go beyond finance, of course. In the military, autonomous drone swarms on land, sea and air are examples of emerging distributed systems that do not require a centralized controller to achieve their mission objectives. In the governance and structure of nation states, commonwealths, confederations, and federations are all examples that exist on the continuum of distributed vs centralized systems. The United States started off being a far more distributed system than it is today. Many more centralized, supra-authorities, laws and regulatory bodies have been added to the governmental framework than envisaged by the founders of the country. Whether good or bad, one must acknowledge the importance of choosing the right structure for a system, business or country. Centralized or distributed paradigms project a structure onto systems, organizations and governments that massively affects the evolution of these entities and the experience of citizens dependent on them.

To centralize or distribute is a fundamental societal design question. Should we empower central banks further by enabling restrictions on distributed stores of value and mediums of exchange, such as cryptocurrency, or should we allow people to use technology to enable exchanges directly? Choosing one or the other has massive implications and shifts economic value and opportunity from banks and middlemen to the parties engaged in transactions. Should we innovate via large, complex, centralized organizations such as NASA or DARPA? Or should we spread resources across dozens or hundreds of companies and university research departments, allowing them to form their own collaborations when scale is needed?

Consider the electric grid, regulators and utilities. All of these operate as fairly centralized structures. During the 2021 winter storm in Texas, it became clear how dependence on centralized structures can spell disaster. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), the overseer of the grid in Texas, was woefully unprepared. And that meant that everyone was unprepared. Millions went without power for days across Texas. Gas prices inflated to $9.99 a gallon, electricity rates approached the stratosphere, hitting $9,000/Mwh, up from $50/Mwh just days before, and even then, homes were subjected to rolling blackouts depriving them of heat, water, communications and the most basic amenities when the temperature outside was -15’ C and the COVID virus ran rampant. Contrast this with many nations in the developing world where homeowners temper their expectations of centralized entities. They simply assume that brownouts and blackouts will occur. They are equipped with solar power, UPSs, generators and other distributed means of production. In a phenomenon that can only be described as “emergent equilibrium”, thousands of distributed power production systems turn on and off to store or produce power, based on the behavior of the centralized grid. This may not be the most efficient system, but it is resilient. And with next generation solar, wind and battery technology, it may well approach the efficiency of a centralized system. At that point, does the centralized system become a liability? Or perhaps it transitions from a system of centralized (some would argue, monopolized) supply to a free market where peer-to-peer exchanges of energy can take place.

Nowhere is the tension between distributed and centralized systems more palpable than in the areas of information, communications and computing. Facebook is a centralized storage system for personal data, pictures, intimate exchanges and geolocation information for over two billion people globally. This database places a tremendous amount of power and control in the hands of a single entity. By not impeding the ability of a single company to gain access to this magnitude of information, we have implicitly allowed such centralized structures to exist. What’s more, we keep replicating them with Whatsapp, TikTok, Tinder, Clubhouse and more. There are distributed social networks, such as Mastodon, where no one entity controls all the information, but these have not taken off yet.

Google is centralized search. Salesforce is a centralized store of commercial opportunities across dozens of industries. Zoom is a centralized multimedia communications service that can route, store, interpret or analyze any exchange that flows through it. It can even send your video to China without you knowing. Cell phone and landline telephones, Whatsapp, SMS text messages, Dropbox, -mail… all these are centralized information systems that are not controlled by the user. For the most part, users didn’t actively choose to structure our information systems in this centralized way. Centralized systems can be more efficient, subject to greater control by a company or government offering the system, and sometimes even easier to use. When they are the only choice and connectivity and information access are fundamental needs, then there is no choice but to flock to them. Distributed systems of exchange have existed and even scaled in the past, but with the advent of portalstyle web destinations, then social networks, and now rampant cloud computing, they’ve mostly fallen by the wayside.

In the 1970s, when point to point connectivity between computer systems facilitated by dialup phone lines was common, the unix-tounix-copy-protocol (UUCP) was a widely used method of peer-topeer exchange of information, email, and other digital assets. Nodes in the network would reach out to one or a few other nodes, which in turn would reach out to others, eventually routing the information and spreading it across the larger network. If one node failed, you would simply go around it. Today, Gmail and Microsoft Exchange 365 host everyone’s e-mail. Do you know with 100% confidence what happens to the information stored there? Do you know, beyond doubt, that no employee or malign actor can access or abuse this information?

The US Government discovered that centralized repositories pose a huge risk to the national security of the country when, in 2015, the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) was hacked and all the data for hundreds of thousands of government employees and contractors, security cleared individuals, was leaked. This included detailed backgrounds, financial summaries, information on families, jobs, contacts; the entire record of their lives in great detail. One would think information like this would be protected, encrypted and secure in the best way possible. But large centralized repositories are awfully hard to secure. They present a massive target and give attackers great rewards due to the bounties they store within. They are like El Dorado, the fabled Aztec City of Gold, and everyone knows the way to them. We should not be surprised when some break in.

Peter Turchin, a professor at the University of Connecticut, is the originator of “Cliodynamics”, a data-based study of factors that contribute to the rise and fall of societies and empires. He posits that it is not a shortage of resources or disparity, per-se, that causes civilizations to crumble. Instead, it is the phenomenon of “elite overproduction”; an inter-elite conflict created when too many relatively rich, upwardly mobile people are produced in a society that offers privileged positions for only a few of them. When cadres of an otherwise educationally enabled and resource-rich elite cannot gain stations to which they aspire, they take to fomenting revolt, rebellion and initiate downward spirals that cause society to sink. Seen in one way, this is nothing other than a consequence of – even the curse of – centralization. A central structure has at its very top, one leader. There are only so many positions that are possible in the second, third and lower rungs. When populations become large, a centralized structure imposes a natural limit on how many people can occupy key positions. It is important to understand that this is a consequence of the centralized structure itself. There is nothing that can be done to alleviate the effect; the effect is built into the structure.

One could therefore conclude that if Turchin’s research and extensive enumeration of civilization-scale catastrophes are to be believed, they result from elite infighting caused by centralized structures. Naturally, as any society develops and becomes more prosperous, the number of people who develop higher aspirations also increases. This is not a terrible thing. But when these aspirations are mixed with structures that impose a natural limit on how many aspirants can have their dreams fulfilled, the result is a toxic, explosive mix. In the prosperous world of 2050, when 10 billion people, enriched by exponential technologies, will reside in our nations and across our continents, can we risk centralized structures that may practically guarantee conflict and instability?

Resolving the distributed vs. centralized question in different contexts seems to be the key civilizational issue we face today. What are the insular, xenophobic chants for ultra-nationalism if not a rejection of the centralized policies, agreements and structures that might govern a comity of nations? What is Bitcoin if not a rejection of government control over monetary expansion and of the credibility of the CPI (Consumer Price Index) as a measure of inflation? What are drone swarms if not a decentralized, distributed attack on centralized platforms, historically, so loved by the military? What is the movement against facial recognition if not a rejection of centralized biometric record keeping which many fear is an attempt to enhance control over populations? What is the #DeleteFacebook campaign if not an expressed aversion to the large scale, centralized harvesting of personal information? And what are thousands of educational YouTube channels, the Khan Academy and dozens of open courseware platforms if not distribution of knowledge that undercuts the monopoly on learning enjoyed by large, centralized universities?

Yesterday, when technology was not sufficiently sophisticated to enable efficiencies of the type we see today, centralization had value. But in a world where direct communications and inexpensive large-scale processing of information is possible and even trivial, does the purpose of centralization devolve to benefitting the entities enabling the centralization? Sadly, one of these “benefits” could be control over end users – the common man – the citizen. This control can be monetized if you are a commercial social network operator or can manifest as suppression if you are a brutal government. But in nearly every case, it now holds little value for the individuals on either end of the exchange. As we discover the brutal aspects of centralized paradigms in a world where large scale information processing and AI are everyday phenomena, I predict we will see society shift to distributed paradigms in most realms to which they can apply.

We are entering such a world. A world not of Global 2000 companies, of 195 countries, of the G-8, or the G-20. But a world of seven billion connected, autonomous human beings participating in an equal exchange. Let us prepare for chaos, the new order.
